content.narrative_summary: The narrative describes diagnosis of non-ischaemic myocardial inflammation by cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) using the updated Lake Louise Criteria (LLC). It states that at least one T2-based criterion plus ideally one T1-based criterion should be met for increased specificity. content.narrative_summary: This page describes the histopathological and molecular diagnostics for myocarditis, including Dallas criteria, immunohistochemistry for CD3+ T cells and CD68+ macrophages, and PCR-based viral nucleic acid detection. It introduces section 4 on the clinical presentation of inflammatory myopericardial syndrome, emphasizing use of “red flags” and risk-based staging (Table 6–7).

content.narrative_summary: Section 4.1 describes that the most common symptom of myocarditis and pericarditis is chest pain (sometimes with infarct-like or pleuritic features) and notes other presentations including dyspnoea, arrhythmias, syncope, and incessant/ongoing IMPS. Section 4.2.1 defines acute myocarditis as symptom duration ≤4 weeks, including fulminant myocarditis, and details the clinical presentation: chest pain in >80% of cases, dyspnoea in 20–50%, fatigue, palpitations, syncope, prodromal symptoms (fever, gastrointestinal or respiratory), and extracardiac signs. It summarizes ECG findings (ST-segment elevation in ~57.5%, other ST/T changes, conduction blocks) and laboratory/echo findings: elevated troponin T/I and CK-MB, echocardiographic signs of myocardial oedema, and pericardial effusion in up to 25% of patients.

content.narrative_summary: Sections describe different stages of myocarditis. Fulminant myocarditis presents in 3–9% of cases with cardiogenic shock, frequent biventricular failure, sustained ventricular arrhythmias, and high risk of sudden cardiac death. Subacute myocarditis lasts 1–3 months with nonspecific symptoms and variable remission or progression. Chronic myocarditis persists beyond 3 months, may cause ventricular remodeling, arrhythmogenic substrate, and often unremarkable symptoms despite underlying dysfunction. Clinical presentations are heterogeneous, with infarct-like chest pain being most common, often following viral infection, with ECG changes and troponin elevation but normal coronary arteries, generally resolving without long-term sequelae in many patients.

Section 4.3.4 reviews sudden cardiac death (SCD) in myocarditis, its incidence in young adults, sex differences, and asymptomatic presentations. Section 4.3.5 discusses the interplay of genetic background and inflammation in myocarditis, highlighting autosomal dominant and recessive gene defects and the higher risk associated with pathogenic/likely pathogenic desmosomal variants, especially DSP, in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). Section 4.4.1 introduces acute pericarditis, its clinical features (pleuritic/positional chest pain, dyspnoea), physical exam findings, ECG changes, and pericardial effusion.

content.narrative_summary: Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic condition characterized by a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium impairing diastolic filling. When associated with pericarditis it is termed CP. Chronic pericardial inflammation leads to scarring, fibrosis, and loss of pericardial elasticity. Main symptoms include dyspnoea, oedema, orthopnoea, and fatigue. The classic presentation features isolated right heart failure with normal or near‐normal natriuretic peptide levels; venous congestion, hepatomegaly, pleural effusions, and ascites can occur. Treatment is empirical anti‐inflammatory therapy, with referral for pericardiectomy without delay if medical therapy fails.

content.narrative_summary: Transient constriction is constrictive pericarditis with ongoing inflammation that can be reversed with anti-inflammatory treatment or may heal spontaneously. It develops with pericarditis, with or without pericardial effusion (about 10% of cases), and resolves with anti-inflammatory therapy in more than 50% of cases. A trial of 3–6 months of anti-inflammatory therapy is recommended in patients with newly diagnosed constrictive pericarditis before referral for pericardiectomy. Biomarkers (e.g., elevated C-reactive protein) and multimodality imaging, including CMR, are mandatory to detect pericardial inflammation. First-line assessment with history, physical examination, ECG, transthoracic echocardiography, laboratory assessment, CT (calcifications), and CMR (inflammation) (Class I). content.narrative_summary: This page defines pericarditis with polyserositis as inflammation of the pericardium with concurrent serous membrane involvement, and distinguishes inflammatory and non-inflammatory phenotypes of pericarditis. The inflammatory phenotype is characterized by systemic inflammation (fever, elevated markers such as C-reactive protein) and responds to anti-inflammatory therapies (e.g., colchicine, anti–IL-1 agents). The non-inflammatory phenotype presents without elevated C-reactive protein or systemic markers (e.g., driven by IL-6 or type I interferon signature) and has unclear pathogenesis. Section 5 begins the diagnostic work-up for suspected IMPS, emphasizing a tailored approach based on clinical severity and risk, including history, exam, biomarkers, ECG, echocardiography, multimodality imaging, and endomyocardial biopsy in selected scenarios. Routine viral serology is not recommended except for HIV, hepatitis C, and suspected bacterial infections (e.g., Borrelia, rickettsial, T. cruzi). Echocardiography is first-line; CMR is an advanced imaging modality; patient-tailored workflow is illustrated in referenced figures and tables.

rows.recommendation: Complete clinical evaluation, including history, physical examination, chest X-ray, biomarkers, ECG, and echocardiography is recommended in all patients with a suspicion of myocarditis and/or pericarditis for the initial diagnostic assessment.
CMR is recommended in patients with the clinical suspicion of myocarditis (using updated LL criteria) and/or pericarditis for the non-invasive diagnosis of inflammatory reaction.
Hospital admission is recommended for patients with high-risk pericarditis for monitoring and treatment.
Hospital admission is recommended for patients with moderate- to high-risk pericarditis for monitoring and treatment.

EMB is recommended in patients with high-risk myocarditis and/or haemodynamic instability, and/or in patients with intermediate-risk myocarditis not responding to conventional therapy in order to detect a specific histologic subtype and to assess the presence of viral genome for treatment.

Invasive coronary angiography or coronary CT, depending on clinical likelihood, is recommended in patients with IMPS if an acute coronary syndrome is suspected to rule out obstructive coronary artery disease.

content.narrative_summary: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is the gold standard for biventricular function quantification and detection of regional wall motion abnormalities. It detects myocardial oedema, hyperaemia, capillary leak, and necrosis/fibrosis via T2-weighted imaging, T2 mapping, T1 mapping, and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), and is useful in non-ischaemic myocardial inflammation and pericardial disease for both diagnosis and follow-up. CMR image quality may be affected by ferromagnetic objects and implants but can be optimized. In intubated or uncooperative patients, fast or motion-corrected techniques can allow imaging. Computed tomography (CT) is established for excluding coronary artery disease, making an aetiological diagnosis in pericardial effusion (e.g., tamponade), assessing pericardial constriction and calcification burden, identifying anatomical abnormalities such as pectus excavatum, and, combined with FDG-PET, aids detection of cardiac sarcoidosis.

content.narrative_summary: Patients with pericarditis who recur during corticosteroid tapering should continue colchicine and receive an NSAID rather than increase steroids, with tapering decisions individualized based on clinical factors (age, renal function, bleeding risk, anticoagulation). content.narrative_summary: IMPS is used as an umbrella term for inflammatory diseases ranging from isolated myocarditis to isolated pericarditis, including overlapping forms. content.narrative_summary: This section discusses giant-cell myocarditis (GCM), a rare autoimmune myocarditis affecting young and middle-aged adults. content.title: 9.4. Myocarditis in sarcoidosis
content.narrative_summary: Cardiac sarcoidosis is an inflammatory heart disease characterized by non-caseating granulomas composed of CD68+ macrophages, CD3+ T lymphocytes, and CD20+ B lymphocytes. Treatment is individualized, targeting inflammation and dysfunction with corticosteroids, device therapy (ICD) for high-risk arrhythmia or reduced LVEF, and, in select cases, transplantation.

content.title: 11.1.3 Therapy
content.narrative_summary: Medical therapy for tuberculous pericarditis consists of a combination of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for at least 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 additional months. Extended therapy beyond 9 months confers no additional benefit and may worsen compliance and cost. Poor penetration of isoniazid into the pericardial space and emerging intracardiac bacillary load underscore the importance of prompt drainage and early antituberculous treatment. Pericardial drainage—by pericardiocentesis or surgical window—is essential for diagnosis and therapy. Constrictive pericarditis develops in up to 50% of untreated cases; adjunctive interventions, such as intrapericardial urokinase and high-dose prednisolone for 6 weeks, may reduce progression. In HIV-infected individuals, corticosteroids carry an increased risk of malignancy and should be used cautiously or avoided.

rows.recommendation: CMR is recommended for follow-up at least within the first 6 months in patients with myocarditis to identify a healed or ongoing process, for risk stratification and personalized therapy, and to enable a return to exercise.

CMR is recommended in patients with suspected pericarditis when a diagnosis cannot be made using clinical criteria to assess evidence of pericardial thickening, oedema, LGE, and to assess the persistence of disease during follow-up in selected cases.
CT is recommended to evaluate pericardial thickness, calcifications, masses, and loculated pericardial effusions, as well as concomitant pleuropulmonary diseases and chest abnormalities.

EMB is recommended in patients with high-risk myocarditis, and/or haemodynamic instability, and/or in patients with intermediate-risk myocarditis not responding to conventional therapy in order to detect a specific histologic subtype and to assess the presence of viral genome for treatment.
Comprehensive autopsy is recommended in all patients <50 years of age with SCD to evaluate the presence of acute myocarditis as a cause and to detect potential underlying inherited cardiac diseases.
Retaining samples suitable for DNA extraction and consulting a cardiac pathologist is recommended in cases of SCD, when an inherited cause is suspected, or the cause of death remains unexplained.
Adherence to the ESC HF guidelines is recommended in cases of myocarditis with LV systolic dysfunction and/or HF to reduce symptoms and to improve LV function.
Routine use of immunosuppressive therapy is not recommended in acute myocarditis with preserved LV function because no outcome benefit has been shown.
Colchicine is recommended as first-line therapy in patients with pericarditis as an adjunct to aspirin/NSAID or corticosteroid therapy to reduce subsequent recurrences.

Anti-IL-1 agents (anakinra or rilonacept) are recommended for patients with recurrent pericarditis after failure of first-line therapies and corticosteroids, and elevation of C-reactive protein levels to reduce recurrences and allow corticosteroid withdrawal.
High-dose aspirin or NSAIDs with proton pump inhibitors are recommended as first-line therapy in patients with pericarditis to control symptoms and reduce recurrences.
Corticosteroids are not recommended as the first option for patients with pericarditis therapy without a specific indication.

A timely and dedicated Shock Team discussion is recommended in patients with myocarditis in the presence of haemodynamic compromise, to decide on the need for escalation to MCS and to determine a long-term management plan.

Pericardiocentesis (echocardiography CT-, or fluoroscopy-guided) is recommended for cardiac tamponade, or suspected bacterial or neoplastic pericarditis, or symptomatic moderate to large pericardial effusion despite medical therapy.

Surgical pericardial drainage is recommended in patients with pericardial effusion when percutaneous pericardiocentesis is not feasible or with purulent pericardial effusion to allow complete drainage and to prevent constriction.
Surgical pleuro-pericardial window is recommended in patients with relapsing pericardial effusion despite medical therapy.
Surgical pericardiectomy is recommended in patients with chronic pericardial constriction or persistent constrictive pericarditis despite medical therapy to improve symptoms and survival.
Tricuspid valve repair is recommended in patients with pericardial constriction and severe tricuspid valve regurgitation to improve symptoms and survival.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with non-active myocarditis and haemodynamically not-tolerated sustained VT to prevent SCD.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents recommendation tables for various forms of myocarditis and pericarditis, including inflammatory myopericardial syndrome, giant-cell myocarditis, sarcoidosis-associated myocarditis (diagnosis and therapy), checkpoint inhibitor–associated myocarditis, inflammatory cardiomyopathy, tuberculous pericarditis (diagnosis and treatment), and neoplastic pericardial involvement. All recommendations are Class I (except one Class III) with Levels of Evidence B or C.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for risk stratification, complications, and outcomes of inflammatory myopericardial syndrome

rows.recommendation: Follow-up with clinical assessment, biomarkers, ECG, exercise test, Holter-ECG monitoring, echocardiography, and CMR at least within 6 months after the index hospitalization is recommended in all patients with myocarditis to identify a potential progression or new risk factors.
Long-term follow-up is recommended for patients with complicated myocarditis to identify a potential progression or new complications.
Long-term follow-up is recommended for patients with incessant or recurrent pericarditis to identify a potential progression and new complications.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for giant-cell myocarditis

rows.recommendation: EMB is recommended in patients with suspected GCM due to unexplained new-onset HF of up to 2 weeks associated with a normal or dilated left ventricle and new ventricular arrhythmias, second- or third-degree AVB, or failure to respond to usual care within 1 to 2 weeks to initiate specific treatment.
Combined immunosuppressive therapy is recommended in patients with a diagnosed GCM.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for myocarditis in sarcoidosis – Diagnosis

rows.recommendation: CMR, using tissue characterization techniques, is recommended in patients with suspected CS to assess cardiac inflammation and myocardial involvement.
18F-FDG-PET is recommended for the diagnostic work-up, including detection of inflammation, as well as for follow-up and assessment of therapeutic response in patients with CS.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for myocarditis in sarcoidosis – Therapy

rows.recommendation: ICD implantation is recommended in patients with CS and sustained ventricular arrhythmia (VT/VF) or aborted CA to prevent SCD.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with CS and LVEF ≤35% to prevent SCD.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis

rows.recommendation: Diagnostic triage within 24 h is recommended in patients with suspected myocarditis induced by ICI to initiate treatment rapidly.

Immediate disruption of ICI and administration of high-dosage corticosteroids are recommended in patients with ICI-associated myocarditis in order to stop the inflammatory reaction and stabilize the patient.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for inflammatory cardiomyopathy

rows.recommendation: Guideline-directed HF treatments are recommended in patients with inflammatory cardiomyopathy to improve and/or stabilize left ventricular function.
Specific medical therapy for the potentially underlying systemic disease is recommended in inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for tuberculous pericarditis – Diagnosis and treatment of tuberculous pericarditis and effusion

rows.recommendation: Diagnostic pericardiocentesis is recommended in all patients with suspected tuberculous pericarditis when diagnosis is not confirmed by non-invasive tests to identify the aetiological agent in pericardial fluid.
Empirical antituberculosis chemotherapy is recommended in patients living in endemic areas with exudative pericardial effusion after excluding other causes to treat the most likely cause.
Standard antituberculosis multidrug treatment for 6 months is recommended in patients with tuberculous pericarditis for the prevention of pericardial constriction.

Pericardiectomy is recommended in patients with tuberculous pericarditis if the condition is not improving or is deteriorating after 4–8 weeks of antituberculosis therapy to change the course of disease.
Empirical antituberculosis treatment is not recommended in patients living in non-endemic areas.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for neoplastic pericardial involvement

rows.recommendation: Pericardiocentesis is recommended for patients with cardiac tamponade to relieve symptoms and establish the diagnosis of malignant pericardial effusion.
Extended pericardial drainage (3–6 days) is recommended in patients with suspected or definite neoplastic pericardial effusion to prevent effusion recurrence.
Cytological analysis of pericardial fluid is recommended in patients with neoplastic pericarditis for the confirmation of malignant pericardial disease.
Systemic antineoplastic treatment is recommended in confirmed cases of neoplastic aetiology to treat the primary and secondary metastatic neoplastic involvement.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for post-cardiac injury syndrome

rows.recommendation: Anti-inflammatory therapy is recommended in patients with PCIS to hasten symptom remission and reduce recurrences.
IL-1 antagonists are recommended in patients with refractory PCIS to prevent recurrences and progression to constriction.
High-dose aspirin is recommended as the first-choice anti-inflammatory therapy for post-myocardial infarction pericarditis and in patients already on antiplatelet therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for purulent pericarditis

rows.recommendation: Urgent pericardiocentesis and/or a surgical window is recommended in patients with suspicion of purulent pericarditis to establish a diagnosis.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for constrictive pericarditis – Diagnosis

rows.recommendation: Multimodality imaging is recommended in all patients with suspected constrictive pericarditis to make the diagnosis and assess pericardial thickening, calcifications, and active inflammation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for constrictive pericarditis – Therapy

rows.recommendation: Anti-inflammatory therapy is recommended in haemodynamically stable patients with a transient or new diagnosis of constriction with concomitant evidence of pericardial inflammation to prevent progression to constriction and avoid pericardiectomy.
Pericardiectomy is recommended in patients with permanent constriction if there is no active inflammation or anti-inflammatory treatment is not successful after 3–6 months.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pregnancy, lactation, and reproductive issues

rows.recommendation: Pre-conception counselling is recommended in women with recurrent pericarditis or myocarditis to assess disease activity and to review therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for physical activity and myocarditis/pericarditis

rows.recommendation: Restriction of physical exercise until remission, for at least 1 month, is recommended in athletes and non-athletes after IMPS using an individualized approach to accelerate recovery.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for multidisciplinary teams in myopericardial syndromes

rows.recommendation: A multidisciplinary team discussion at a referral centre is recommended in patients with high-risk/complicated IMPS to provide a patient-tailored approach.
